bfs(G, src):
    Input: graph G, starting vertex src

    create predecessor array, initialised to -1
    create queue Q

    predecessor[src] = src
    enqueue src into Q

    while Q is not empty:
        v = dequeue from Q
        for each neighbour w of v in G where predecessor[w] = -1:
            predecessor[w] = v
            enqueue w into Q

dijkstra(G, src):
    Input: graph G, source vertex src

    create dist array, initialised to inf
    create pred array, initialised to -1
    create vSet containing all vertices of G
    dist[src] = 0

    while vSet is not empty:
        find vertex v in vSet such that dist[v] is minimal
        remove v from vSet

        for each edge (v, w, weight) in G:
            if dist[v] + weight < dist[w]:
                dist[w] = dist[v] + weight
                pred[w] = v

blocks.source_text:
kruskalMst(G):
    Input:  graph G with V vertices
    Output: minimum spanning tree of G

    mst = empty graph with V vertices
    sortedEdges = sort edges of G by weight

    for each edge (v, w, weight) in sortedEdges:
        if there is no path between v and w in mst:
            add edge (v, w, weight) to mst
            if mst has V - 1 edges:
                return mst

    no mst

primMst(G):
    Input:  graph G with V vertices
    Output: minimum spanning tree of G

    mst = empty graph with V vertices
    usedV = {0}
    unusedE = edges of G

    while |usedV| < V :
        find cheapest edge e (s, t, weight) in unusedE such that
            s in usedV and t not in usedV
        add e to mst
        add t to usedV
        remove e from unusedE

    return mst

blocks.source_text:
How to write a recursive function:
First, think:
- How can the solution be expressed in terms of subproblems?
- What would the subproblem(s) be?
- How can the original problem be related to the subproblem(s)?
- What are the base cases?
Then, implement:
- Implement base case(s) first.
- Then implement recursive cases.
- Each subproblem corresponds to a recursive call.
- Assume that the function works for the subproblem(s).

partition(t, i):
    Input: tree t, index i
    Output: tree with i-th item moved to root
    leftSize = size(t->left)
    if i < leftSize:
        t->left = partition(t->left, i)
        t = rotateRight(t)
    else if i > leftSize:
        t->right = partition(t->right, i - leftSize - 1)
        t = rotateLeft(t)
    return t

blocks.title: Graph fundamentals and terminology - lecture
blocks.displayed_language_inference: Pseudocode/prose flag
blocks.content_kind_inference: Pseudocode or conceptual prose, as declared
blocks.source_text:
A graph consists of:
- a set of vertices V (also called nodes)
- a set of edges E between pairs of vertices

Course terminology:
- vertices are usually integers from 0 to |V| - 1
- edges may be directed, weighted and/or labelled
- a loop is an edge from a vertex to itself
- a simple graph is undirected, has no loops and has no multiple edges
- vertices are adjacent when an edge connects them; degree counts incident edges
- a path follows edges; a simple path has no repeating vertices; a cycle starts and ends at the same vertex
- a complete graph connects every pair of vertices
- a connected graph has a path between every pair of vertices
- a tree is connected and has no cycles
- a connected component is a maximally connected subgraph
- a spanning tree contains all vertices and is a single tree
- a spanning forest contains one tree for each connected component
- a clique is a complete subgraph

blocks.title: Directed terminology - exact lecture concept
blocks.displayed_language_inference: Pseudocode/prose flag
blocks.content_kind_inference: Pseudocode or conceptual prose, as declared
blocks.source_text:
Directed graph terminology:
- each edge (v, w) has source v and destination w
- in-degree is the number of incoming edges
- out-degree is the number of outgoing edges
- a directed path follows outgoing edges
- w is reachable from v when there is a directed path from v to w
- a digraph is strongly connected when there is a directed path from every vertex to every other vertex
- a strongly-connected component is a maximally strongly-connected subgraph

blocks.title: Spanning-forest edge recording - supplemental
blocks.displayed_language_inference: Pseudocode/prose flag
blocks.content_kind_inference: Added teaching C bridge
blocks.source_text:
spanningForest(G):                    # supplemental extension of components(G)
    create componentOf array, initialised to -1
    create empty treeEdges list
    compNo = 0
    for each vertex v in G:
        if componentOf[v] = -1:
            dfsForest(G, v, componentOf, compNo, treeEdges)
            compNo = compNo + 1
    return componentOf, treeEdges

dfsForest(G, v, componentOf, compNo, treeEdges):
    componentOf[v] = compNo
    for each neighbour w of v in G:
        if componentOf[w] = -1:
            add edge (v, w) to treeEdges      # a tree edge of component compNo
            dfsForest(G, w, componentOf, compNo, treeEdges)

Invariant
    The recorded edges form a spanning forest of G: one spanning tree per
    connected component, and no cycle, because an edge is recorded only when
    it reaches a vertex whose componentOf is still -1.
    A spanning forest of a graph with V vertices and C components has exactly
    V - C edges. A tree on k vertices has k - 1 edges, so adding up over the
    C components gives (sum of the k) - C = V - C.
    A component of one vertex is a tree on one vertex and contributes 0 edges,
    so an isolated vertex still counts towards both V and C.
    An input edge that is not recorded is a non-tree edge. In an undirected
    DFS a non-tree edge closes a cycle inside its own component, and the
    number of non-tree edges is E - (V - C).

    reached exactly once and the step number is unique.

deleteBackshift(ht, key):
    i = the slot holding key, found along key's own probe sequence
    if key is absent:
        return                                 # table unchanged
    empty slot i                               # no deleted marker is written
    hole = i
    j = i
    repeat numSlots - 1 times:
        j = (j + 1) mod numSlots               # walk forwards through the cluster
        if slot j is empty:
            stop                               # the cluster ends at a real hole
        k = the key stored in slot j
        if probeStep(k, hole) < probeStep(k, j):
            move k from slot j into slot hole  # its probe path crossed the hole
            empty slot j
            hole = j

For linear probing the stride is 1, so probeStep(k, s) is just the forward
distance from hash(k) to s, and the test reduces to "the hole lies between
this key's home slot and the slot it now occupies". The cluster scan then
repairs every probe path the deletion could have broken, which is why
backshift leaves no marker behind at all.

With double hashing a probe path jumps across the table, so a key whose path
crosses the emptied slot need not sit in the cluster behind it. The
implementation therefore finishes with a verification sweep: every live key is
looked up, and any key that is no longer reachable is lifted out and
re-inserted along its own probe sequence. For linear probing the sweep never
finds one. For double hashing it is the extra work that is exactly why the
lecture pairs backshift with linear probing and keeps the tombstone as the
general method.

Cost
    backshift   O(cluster length) at delete time, and keys move, so any index
                stored into the table is invalidated. No later lookup pays.
    tombstone   O(probe length) at delete time and nothing moves, but every
                later lookup must probe through each marker, and the markers
                accumulate until the table is rebuilt.

Cluster measurement
    cluster       a maximal run of consecutive occupied slots, wrapping round
                  the end of the table. A deleted marker counts as occupied,
                  because a lookup must still probe through it.
    longest run   the number of slots in the largest such run
    mean probes   the total number of slots probed to look up every live key
                  once, divided by the number of live keys

Linear probing puts a colliding key at the end of whichever run it lands in,
so neighbouring runs merge and the longest run grows. That growth is primary
clustering, and it is what makes the mean probe length rise faster than the
load factor alone would suggest.
Double hashing gives each key its own stride, so two keys with the same home
slot separate after one probe instead of becoming adjacent, and a single run
does not grow. The stride is the reason, not luck.
